(A13) Domain Density (arithmetic circuit)
Given: An arithmetic circuit (with division gate and sign function), defining a (partial) function f ∶ Rn → R.
Question: Is the domain of f dense in Rn ?
Complexity: ∀R-complete, by Bürgisser, Cucker [BC09, Proposition 5.7, Corollary 9.4].
Comments: In the Zariski topology, Bürgisser, Cucker [BC09, Proposition 5.7, Corollary 9.4] show that
     the problem is ∃R-complete.
Also see: Image density (second level) (A45), density of semialgebraic set (A34).

(A14) Polynomial Projection (Linear)
Given: Two polynomials f, g ∶ Rn → R in Z[x1 , x2 , . . . , xn ].
Question: Is there a matrix A such that f (x) = g(Ax)?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Bläser, Rao, and Sarma [BRS17] via a reduction from the symmetric tensor
     rank problem (A26) .
Comments: Over an arbitrary integral domain, the problem is complete for the existential theory of that
     domain [BRS17]. If A is a diagonal, invertible matrix, then the polynomial projection problem can be
     solved in randomized polynomial time [BRS17]. The general (affine) polynomial projection problem
     asks whether there is a matrix A and a vector b such that f (x) = g(Ax + b). The special case A = I is
     known as polynomial equivalence under shifts (A-Open2).
Open Questions: Is the affine polynomial projection problem ∃R-hard? This version is known to be NP-
     hard by Kayal [Kay12].
Also see: Polynomial equivalence under shifts (A-Open2).

15.2      Matrices and Tensors
       A d-dimension (real) tensor T is an element in Rn1 ×⋯×nd . The tensor has rank at most k if it
       can be written as ∑ki=1 v1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ vk , where vi ∈ Rni for 1 ≤ i ≤ d, and ⊗ is the outer product of two
       vectors. Matrices are then the special case of 2-dimensional tensors. There are other notions of
       tensor- and matrix-rank, some of which we discuss below.

(A15) Matrix Singularity
Given: A square matrix M (x1 , . . . , xk ) with variable entries x1 , . . . , xk and entries in Q.
Question: Is M (x1 , . . . , xk ) singular, that is, does M (x1 , . . . , xk ) have determinant 0 for some (x1 , . . . , xk ) ∈ Rk ?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Buss, Frandsen, Shallit [BFS99] via a reduction from Feasibility (A1).
Comments: Buss, Frandsen, Shallit [BFS99] show that the singularity problem over any commutative ring
     R is complete for the existential theory of R. The reduction is based on Valiant’s universality proof
     for the determinant [Val79]. Non-singularity, that is, testing whether M (x1 , . . . , xk ) is non-singular for
     some x1 , . . . , xk lies in randomized polynomial time, so is unlikely to be ∃R-complete [BFS99]. Brijder,
     Geerts, and Van den Bussche [BGVdBW19] introduce a formal matrix language (MATLANG) in which
     matrix singularity is expressible, implying that expression evaluation in that language is ∃R-complete.
Also see: Existential theory of invertible matrices (L-Open2), constrained matrix invertibility problem (A-
     Open7), feasibility (A1).

(A16) Minimum/Maximum Matrix Rank
Given: A square matrix M (x1 , . . . , xk ) variable entries x1 , . . . , xk and entries in Q, integer k.
Question: Is the rank of M (x1 , . . . , xk ) at most/at least k for some (x1 , . . . , xk ) ∈ Rk ?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Buss, Frandsen, Shallit [BFS99] via a reduction from Feasibility (A1).
Comments: Buss, Frandsen, Shallit [BFS99] show that the minimum and maximum matrix rank problems
     over any field F is complete for the existential theory of F , even if the matrix entries lie in {0, 1}. A
     minimum rank problem for matrices with affine entries can be used to prove ∃R-completeness of tensor
     rank (A26), see [SŠ18].
Open Questions: Buss, Frandsen, Shallit [BFS99] show that approximating the minimum rank of a matrix
     to within a factor of 1 + ε is NP-hard for sufficiently small ε, is it also ∃R-hard? ▼ How hard is the
     minimum matrix rank problem if each variable occurs only once in the matrix? This is the well-known
     minimum rank matrix completion problem, the maximum rank version of this problem can be solved
     in randomized polynomial time [BFS99]. Related to this is the problem of computing the minimum
     rank of a sign pattern matrix (A18). ▼ Is the problem hard for constant k, say k = 4?
Also see: Feasibility (A1), tensor rank (A26), minimum rank of sign pattern matrix (A18), minimum graph
     rank (A20), low rank approximation (matrix) (A-Open8).

(A17) Minimum Rank of Linear Combination of Matrices
Given: A family of matrices M1 , M2 , . . . , Mk ∈ Qm×n and an integer r.
Question: Is the rank of ∑i λi Mi at most r for some nonzero combination (λ1 , . . . , λk ) ∈ Rk ?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Bläser, Ikenmeyer, Lysikov, Pandey, and Schreyer [BIL+ 21, Theorem 2.3] via
     a reduction from H2 N (A6) even for r = 1.
Comments: There are interesting connections to various notions of tensor rank, including slice rank and
     border rank, see [BIL+ 21]. The result is used to prove ∃R-hardness of the orbit closure containment
     problem (A28).
Open Questions: There is an affine version of this problem, in which we require that λ1 = 1; this version
     is known to be NP-hard [BIJL18], but is it ∃R-complete?
Also see: Minimum matrix rank (A16), tensor rank (A26), orbit closure containment (A28).

(A18) Minimum Rank of Sign Pattern Matrix
Given: A generalized sign pattern matrix, that is, M ∈ {+, −, 0}n×n , integer k.

Question: Is there a matrix A ∈ Rn×n of rank at most k so that sgn(A) = M , where sgn is the sign function
     applied to each entry?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Bhangale, Kopparte [BK15] via a reduction from simple stretchability (CG9),
     even for k = 3.
Comments: For k = 2 the problem is solvable in polynomial time [BK15]. The maximum rank variant is
     equivalent to a matching problem and can be solved in polynomial time [BK15].
Open Questions: Generalized in the name refers to allowing the entry 0; in a sign pattern matrix zero
     entries are not allowed; in this case Bhangale, Kopparte [BK15] can still show that the problem is

Also see: Minimum/maximum matrix rank (A16), feasibility (A1).

(A19) Monotone Matrix Rank
Given: A matrix M ∈ Qm×n , integer k.
Question: Is the monotone rank of M at most k, that is, is there a matrix A of rank at most k, and

(A20) Minimum Graph Rank
Given: A graph G on n vertices, an integer k ≥ 0.
Question: Is there a real symmetric matrix A ∈ Rn×n of rank at most k so that vi vj ∈ E(G) if and only if
     Ai,j ≠ 0, for 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n?
Complexity: ∃R-complete even for k = 3 by Grace, Hall, Jensen and Lawrence [Law23, Section 4] via a
     reduction from feasibility (A1).
Comments: It is also claimed that over an arbitrary infinite field instead of R, the problem (with A being
     Hermitian instead of symmetric) is equivalent to the existential theory of the field.
Also see: Minimum matrix rank (A16).

(A21) Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
Given: A square matrix M ∈ Qn×n with all entries non-negative and a natural number k ∈ N.
Question: Are there n × k and k × n matrices A, B such that M = AB and all entries of A and B are
     non-negative?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Shitov [Shi16b] via a reduction from feasibility (A1).
Comments: Vavasis had earlier shown NP-hardness [Vav09]. The smallest k for which M has a non-negative
     factorization equals the non-negative rank of M , that is the smallest number of rank-1 matrices with
     non-negative entries, whose sum is M [CR93, Lemma 2.1], so the non-negative matrix rank problem is
     also ∃R-complete. Rank problems for matrices with affine entries can be used to prove ∃R-completeness
     of tensor rank (A26), see [SŠ18].
Universality: Shitov [Shi16b] also shows universality.
Open Questions: Is the problem already hard for some fixed k, say four?
Also see: Nested polytopes (CG71), Hadamard decomposition (A-Open9).

(A22) (Real) PSD Rank
Given: A matrix A ∈ Qm×n , a natural number r ∈ N.
Question: Is psd-rank(A) ≤ r? That is, are there Hermitian positive semidefinite r×r matrices (B1 , . . . , Bm )
    and (C1 , . . . , Cn ) with A(i, j) = trace(Bi Cj ), for all i, j? If the Bi and Cj are restricted to be real, we
    obtain the real psd rank of A.

Complexity: Shitov established ∃R-completeness [Shi23, Theorem 3.4] of the (complex) PSD rank. He

(A24) Phaseless Rank

Complexity: Shitov established ∃R-completeness [Shi23, Theorem 3.7].
Comments: The problem is hard even if the numerator and denominator of each entry are given in unary.

(A25) Rank-Constrained Optimization
Given: Two matrices A, B ∈ Rℓ×n , a natural number k.
Question: Is there an n × n matrix X in the positive semidefinite cone S+n such that AX = B and rank(X) ≤

Complexity: ∃R-complete by Bertsimas, Cory-Wright, and Pauphilet [BCWP22] via a reduction from
     linkage realizability (CG65).

     ⟨C, X⟩ + λ ⋅ rank(X) subject to AX = B, rank(X) ≤ k and X ∈ K for some proper cone K is considered.

Also see: Linkage realizability (CG65).

(A26) Tensor Rank
Given: A 3-dimensional tensor T = (tijk ) ∈ Qd1 ×d2 ×d3 , a natural number k.
Question: Is the (tensor) rank of T at most k; that is, are there at most k rank-1 tensors T1 , . . . , Tk such
    that T = ∑i∈[k] Ti ? A tensor has rank-1 if it can be written as u ⊗ v ⊗ w for real vectors u, v, w, where
    ⊗ is the outer (Kronecker) product of two vectors.
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Schaefer, Štefankovič [SŠ18] via a reduction from a restricted version of the
    minimum matrix rank problem (A16), and Shitov [Shi16a] via a reduction from feasibility (A1). The

Comments: Tensor rank was famously shown NP-hard by Håstad [Hås90]. Shitov [Shi16a] showed that
    over an integral domain, the (symmetric) tensor rank problem is as hard as the existential theory of
    that domain. For a related notion, called border rank, whose complexity is still open, see [BIJL18].
Universality: There is a universality result [SŠ24] (which fixes the version in [SŠ18]).

15.3      Semialgebraic and Algebraic Sets
       For polynomials and their representations, see Section 15. An algebraic set is the zero-set of
       a family of polynomials: S = {x ∈ Rn ∶ fi (x) = 0 for all i ∈ [k]} and is specified by its defining
       polynomials, fi , i ∈ [k]. A basic semialgebraic set is a set of the form S = {x ∶∈ Rn ∶ fi (x) = 0 for all
       i ∈ [k], gi (x) > 0 for all i ∈ [m]}. A semialgebraic set is the finite union of basic semialgebraic sets.
       We will see two ways of specifying a semialgebraic set: via a formula φ as S = {x ∈ Rn ∶ φ(x)},
       where φ is a quantifier-free formula in the theory of the reals with free variables x; and via an
       arithmetic circuit C, where S = {x ∶∈ Rn ∶ C(x) = 1}, where x are the variables of the circuit C.
       Unless we say otherwise, we assume a semialgebraic set is specified using the formula φ.

(A29) Cardinality of Semialgebraic Set
Given: A semialgebraic set S ⊆ Rn , a natural number k ≥ 1 or k = ∞.
Question: Does S contain fewer than k elements?
Complexity: ∀R-complete by Cucker and Rosselló [CR92] via a reduction from feasibility (A1) for any
     fixed k, including k = ∞.
Comments: Special (named) cases are k = 1, the emptiness and k = ∞, the finiteness problem. Cucker
     and Rosselló [CR92] work in the BSS-model, but their proof carries over to ∀R. If k is not fixed, the
     problem is complete for the counting version of ∃R, see [BC06, Proposition 8.5(ii)].
Also see: Dimension of semialgebraic set (A30), feasibility (A1).

(A30) Dimension of Semialgebraic Set
Given: A semialgebraic set S ⊆ Rn , an integer d ≥ 0.

Schaefer, Cardinal, Miltzow                                                                  ∃R Compendium


Question: Does S have (real) dimension at least d; that is, is there a projection π ∶ Rn → Rd (dropping
    n − d coordinates), such that π(S) contains a non-empty interior?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Koiran [Koi99] via reduction from feasibility (A1), even for any fixed d ≥ 0.
Comments: For d = 0 the problem degenerates to the non-emptiness problem of a semialgebraic set (A29).
    Cucker and Rosselló [CR92] looked at the cases d = n−1, which they call the hypersurface problem, and
    d = n, which they call the NEI (nonempty interior) problem. They showed that both problems can be
    described using the exotic quantifier ∃∗ (not formally introduced until Koiran’s papers [Koi99, Koi00]).
     The ∃R-hardness reduction is straight-forward, the non-trivial part is showing that the problem lies in
     ∃R. Koiran [Koi99] first shows this for the BSS-model, but also explains how to translate the result into
     the discrete setting, corresponding to ∃R. Koiran had earlier shown that the complex dimension of a
     semialgebraic set is ∃C-complete (again for the BSS-model) [Koi97b]. For his result Koiran introduces
     the exotic quantifier ∃∗ and shows how to eliminate it.
Also see: Local dimension of semialgebraic set (A31), feasibility (A1).

(A31) Local Dimension of Semialgebraic Set

Complexity: ∃R-complete by Bürgisser and Cucker [BC09, Corollary 6.6,Corollary 9.4] even for d = 1 via
     a reduction from testing whether 0 lies in the closure of a semialgebraic set (A37).

Also see: Dimension of semialgebraic set (A30).

(A35) Diameter of Semialgebraic Set

Question: Does S have diameter at most d; that is, do every two points in S have distance at most d from

Complexity: ∀R-complete by Schaefer, Štefankovič [SŠ23] via reduction from Feasibility (A1) over a
     bounded domain.
Comments: The strict version, in which we require the diameter to be strictly less than d is also ∀R-
     complete; the only issue is ∀R-membership, but that can be handled using the exotic H-quantifier as
     we saw in Section 2.4.
Also see: Radius of semialgebraic set (A34).

(A36) Density of Semialgebraic Set
Given: A semialgebraic set S ⊆ Rn .
Question: Is S dense in Rn ? A set S ⊆ T is dense in T if for every t ∈ T and every ε > 0 there is an s ∈ S
    such that ∥s − t∥ < ε.
Complexity: In ∀R by Koiran [Koi99]. ∀R-complete by Bürgisser, Cucker [BC09, Proposition 5.2,Corollary
    9.3], and Schaefer, Štefankovič [SŠ23] via reduction from strict positivity over a bounded domain.
Comments: The tricky part here is membership in ∀R, that follows using Koiran’s method [Koi99]. Bür-
    gisser, Cucker [BC09] showed the problem complete for semialgebraic sets defined by arithmetic circuits,
    Schaefer, Štefankovič [SŠ23] strengthened the result to semialgebraic sets defined by formulas.
     The directed Hausdorff distance of S and T (A43) is 0 if and only if S ∩ T is dense in T , so replacing
     Rn with another semialgebraic set leads to a ∀∃R-complete problem.
Open Questions: Does the problem remain hard for algebraic sets?
Also see: Distance of semialgebraic sets (A40), (directed) Hausdorff distance of semialgebraic sets (second
     level) (A43), zero in closure of semialgebraic set (A37), Image density (second level) (A45), Domain
     density (arithmetic circuit) (A13).

(A37) Zero in Closure of Semialgebraic Set
Given: A semialgebraic set S ⊆ Rn .
Question: Does 0 belong to the closure of S? That is, are there sn ∈ S such that ∥si ∥ → 0 for n → ∞?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Cucker, Rosselló [CR92].
Comments: Membership is the interesting result here, it requires an upper bound from real algebraic geome-
     try. Cucker and Rosselló [CR92] call this the (Euclidean) adherence problem. Bürgisser, Cucker [BC09,
     Proposition 5.1,Corollary 9.4] study both the Euclidean and Zariski adherence problem.
Open Questions: How hard is this problem in the Zariski topology [BC09, Table 2]?
Also see: Distance of semialgebraic sets (A40).

(A38) Isolated Point of Semialgebraic Set
Given: A semialgebraic set S ⊆ Rn .
Question: Is 0 an isolated point in S, that is, does S not contain other points arbitrarily close to 0?
Complexity: ∀R-complete by Bürgisser, Cucker [BC09, Corollary 6.7, Corollary 9.4] via a reduction from
     testing whether 0 lies in the closure of a semialgebraic set (A37).
Comments: The problem remains hard for algebraic sets, see the isolated zero problem (A7). The com-
     plexity of testing whether a semialgebraic set contains an isolated point is open (A-Open3).
Also see: Isolated zero (A7), semialgebraic set with isolated point (A-Open3), zero in closure of semialge-
     braic set (A37).

Question: Is B closed, that is, does it contain all its limit points?

16      Computational Geometry
16.1      Realizability of Configurations
       A rank-d chirotope is a function χ ∶ {1, 2, . . . , n}d ∶→ {−1, 0, 1} with the following properties: (i)
       exchanging two components i and j changes the sign: χ(τij (λ)) = −χ(λ) , hence it is an alternating
       sign map; (ii) the function ∣χ∣ is the characteristic function of independent sets of a matroid ; (iii)
       the following Grassmann-Plücker relation holds: for every λ ∈ [n]d−2 and a, b, c, d ∈ [n] ∖ λ, the
       set
                        {χ(λ, a, b) ⋅ χ(λ, c, d), −χ(λ, a, c) ⋅ χ(λ, b, d), χ(λ, a, d) ⋅ χ(λ, b, c)}
       either contains {−1, +1} or equals {0}. We usually identify a chirotope χ with it opposite −χ. A
       chirotope defines an oriented matroid of rank d. In rank three, chirotopes are often referred to as
       order types. it can be checked that for a given set of n vectors {v1 , v2 , . . . , vn } in Rd , the function
       χ that returns sgn(det(vλ1 , vλ2 , . . . , vλd )) satisfies the above properties. This function indicates
       the orientation of the simplex formed by any d-tuple of vectors. In the plane, we can associate to
       every point p ∈ R2 the vector (p1 , p2 , 1). Then the rank-three chirotope given by the determinant
       indicates whether a given ordered triple of points forms a clockwise, counter-clockwise, or flat
       triangle. It is not true that every rank-three chirotope corresponds to a set of points in the plane,
       in that sense. Deciding this is one of the fundamental ∃R-complete problem.

(CG1) (Simple) Order Type Realizability
Given: An order type χ ∶ [n]3 ∶→ {−1, 0, 1}.


                                                            50
Schaefer, Cardinal, Miltzow                                                                          ∃R Compendium


Question: Are there points p1 , . . . , pn in the plane realizing this order type, hence such that pk lies to
     the left of pi pj if χ(pi , pj , pk ) = −1, to the right if χ(pi , pj , pk ) = 1, and the three points are collinear
     otherwise?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Mnëv [Mnë88, Sho91] even if the order type is simple (aka uniform), that is,
     does not take on value 0.
Comments: This is one of the original ∃R-complete problems, dual to simple stretchability (CG9), and a
     special case of (rank-3) oriented matroid realizability. For a detailed proof of ∃R-completeness, see
     Matoušek [Mat14]. In spatial reasoning, the order type is captured by the LR-calculus (left/right
     calculus, (L10)), which is therefore ∃R-complete [WL10]. There is a partial variant, in which χ is
     only required to be defined on subsets of [n] of fixed size and fixed overlap; that version remains
     ∃R-complete [Sch21b], which is useful in establishing results for problems with fixed parameters, such
     as segment intersection graphs of bounded degree (CG25), pseudo-segment stretchability (CG10), and
     the rectilinear local crossing number (CG51).
Universality: Mnëv [Mnë88], also see Shor [Sho91].
Also see: Directional walk (CG6), collinearity logic (L9), LR-calculus (L10), pseudo-segment stretchabil-
     ity (CG10), rectilinear local crossing number (CG51).

(CG2) Oriented Matroid Realizability Over the Reals
Given: A rank-d oriented matroid, for some fixed d, given for example as a chirotope χ ∶ [n]d → {−1, 0, 1}.
Question: Can this oriented matroid be realized over the reals, hence are there vectors v1 , . . . , vn ∈ Rd such
     that χ(λ) = sgn(det(vλ1 , vλ2 , . . . , vλd ))?
Complexity: ∃R-complete from order type realizability (CG1).
Also see: Order type realizability (CG1).

(CG3) Matroid Realizability Over the Reals
Given: A family F ⊂ 2[n] and a dimension d ∈ N.
Question: Are there vectors v1 , . . . , vn ∈ Rd such that for every set s ∈ 2[n] , we have s ∈ F if and only if the
    vectors {vi ∶ i ∈ S} are linearly independent?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Kim, Mesmay, and Miltzow [KdMM23]; the paper contains two reductions:
    one from order type realizability (CG1), the other from distinct ETR (L4).
Comments: The proof follows from a careful reading of the ∃R-completeness proofs of order type realizabil-
    ity (CG1) [Mat14], but the result was first explicitly stated by Kim, Mesmay, and Miltzow [KdMM23]
    in an arguably simpler and self-contained way. Matroids can be represented in various ways, affecting
    the complexity status of the realizability problem. Typically matroids are given by a circuit or black-
    box model. Compared to that, the explicit representation via independent sets may appear wasteful.
    However, representing the problem explicitly an only make it easier, but it is still ∃R-hard. Moreover,
    matroid realizability is ∃R-complete for every fixed d ≥ 3, so at most O(nd ) sets have to be specified.
     Sturmfels also studied the problem of matroid realizability over the rational numbers and showed similar
     equivalences with finding rational solutions to Diophantine equations [Stu87]. However Sturmfels’
     reduction is not polynomial time, so does not establish an ∃Q-completeness result.
Also see: Order type realizability (CG1), distinct ETR (L4).

(CG4) (Simple) Allowable Sequence
Given: A sequence π1 , . . . , πk of permutations of [n].
Question: Is the given sequence allowable, that is, is there a set of n points in the plane so that the
    permutations π1 , . . . , πk are obtained, in that order, by projecting the points onto a line rotating by a
    half turn around some point of the plane?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Hoffmann and Merckx [HM18] even if the sequence is simple, that is, every
    two consecutive permutations differ by transposition of two adjacent elements via a reduction from
    order type realizability (CG1).

Comments: Allowable sequences are one of the oldest tools in the computational geometers tool set, first
     introduced in the 19th century, see [GP80].

Also see: Order type realizability (CG1), visibility graph of polygon with holes (CG36).

(CG5) Radial System Realizability
Given: An (abstract) radial system, that is a family (πi )i∈[n] such that πi is a permutation of [n] − {i}, for

     clockwise order as described by πi ?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Cardinal and Kusters [CK15] via a reduction from order type realizabil-
     ity (CG1).
Comments: There is a partial variant, in which the radial system only needs to be specified for point sets of

     lems with fixed parameters, such as existence of simultaneous geometric embeddings for a fixed number
     of graphs, and straight-line realizability of bounded-degree graphs with rotation system (CG54).

(CG6) Directional Walk
Given: A walk W on n vertices, and a direction left/right for every triple of consecutive points along W .
Question: Are there n points in the plane so that for all triples (p, q, r) of consecutive points along the
     walk, r lies to the left or right or pq as specified and distinct vertices are mapped to distinct locations?
Complexity: ∃R-complete [Sch21b] via a reduction from a partial version of order type realizability (CG1).
     Remains ∃R-complete even if each edge occurs at most once on the walk [KR23].
Comments: The directional walk problem can be viewed as a sparsified version of order type realizability,
     or a special case of the left/right calculus [WL10].
Open Questions: Does the problem remain ∃R-complete if the realizing walk has to be crossing-free? ▼
     The proof in [Sch21b] implies that the problem remains ∃R-complete even if each vertex occurs only a
     finite number of times along the walk. Is the directional walk problem ∃R-complete even if each vertex
     occurs at most twice (once being trivial)?
Also see: Order type realizability (CG1).

(CG7) Finite Convex Geometry Realizability
Given: A finite convex geometry (V, C), that is a set C ⊆ 2V that contains ∅, V , is closed under intersection,

Question: Are there n points in Rd which realize the given finite convex geometry? Letting conv(C)
     denote the convex hull of the points in C, a point set P realizes the finite convex geometry (P, {C ⊆
     P ∶ conv(C) ∩ P = C}).
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Adaricheva and Wild [AW10, HM18] for d = 2, via a reduction from order
     type realizability (CG1), and by Hoffmann and Merckx [HM18] for d ≥ 2 via a reduction from allowable
     sequence (CG4).
Also see: Allowable sequence (CG4), order type realizability (CG1), convex neural codes (CG-Open9).

Complexity: ∃R-complete for every d ≥ 2 by Akitaya, Buchin, Mirzanezhad, Ryvkin, and Wenk [ABM+ 23,

16.2     Arrangements and Stretchability
       Arrangements of vectors or points can be dualized into arrangements of hyperplanes. From the
       topological representation theorem [FL78, BKMS05], oriented matroids can always be realized
       as arrangements of pseudo-hyperplanes. In the planar case, we obtain pseudoline arrangements.
       In a projective setting, a pseudoline arrangement is defined on a two-sphere, but a pseudoline
       arrangement can also be defined in the plane as a collection of x-monotone curves that pairwise
       intersect exactly once. For our purpose, the only relevant information about a pseudoline ar-
       rangement is the underlying combinatorics, or equivalence class under homeomorphisms of the
       plane. A convenient way to specify this information is in the form of a wiring diagram, or by
       specifying, for each pseudoline, the left-to-right order of its intersection points with the other
       pseudolines.
(CG9) (Pseudoline) Stretchability
Given: A pseudoline arrangement.
Question: Is the arrangement stretchable, that is, is it isomorphic to a straight-line arrangement?
Complexity: ∃R-complete, by Mnëv [Mnë88], and Shor [Sho91] via a reduction from the existential theory
     of totally ordered real variables (L2). The problem remains ∃R-complete if the given arrangement is
     simple, that is, at most two pseudolines intersect in each point [SŠ17]. Since simple stretchability in
     the plane is equivalent to simple stretchability in the hyperbolic plane, hyperbolic simple stretchability
     is also ∃R-complete [Bie22, BBDJ23].
Comments: Stretchability is the original ∃R-complete problem in the Mnëv/Shor tradition. Mnëv [Mnë88]
     showed that pseudoline stretchability is universal, and Shor [Sho91] recast the result from a computer
     scientists point of view. A nice introductory presentation of the result is due to Matoušek [Mat14].
     Shor [Sho91] also explicitly shows that pseudo-line stretchability is NP-hard.
Universality: Both pseudoline stretchability and simple pseudoline stretchability are universal, as shown
     by Mnëv [Mnë88], also see Shor [Sho91].
Also see: Existential theory of totally ordered real variables (L2), pseudo-segment stretchability (CG10).
(CG10) Pseudo-segment Stretchability
Given: An arrangement of pseudo-segments: x-monotone curves such that each pair intersects exactly once.
Question: Is the arrangement stretchable, that is, is it isomorphic to an arrangement of straight-line seg-
     ments?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Mnëv [Mnë88], and Shor [Sho91], since pseudoline stretchability (CG9) can
     be viewed as a special case. The problem remains ∃R-complete if each pseudo-segment is involved
     in at most 72 crossings and the arrangement is simple, by Schaefer [Sch21b] via a reduction from a
     partial version of order type realizability (CG1). Förster, Kindermann, Miltzow, Parada, Terziadis,
     and Vogtenhuber [FKM+ 24] show that the problem remains ∃R-hard even if the intersection graph of
     the arrangement has chromatic number at most 30.
Comments: This result can be used to show that segment intersection graphs (CG25) of degree at most
     216 are ∃R-complete to recognize [Sch21b] and that the geometric thickness of multigraphs (CG56) is
     ∃R-complete [FKM+ 24].
Open Questions: What is the smallest number of crossings on a pseudo-segment for which the pseudo-
     segment stretchability remains ∃R-complete? ▼ Does the problem remain ∃R-complete if the intersec-
     tion graph of the arrangement has chromatic number at most 2? [FKM+ 24].
Also see: Order type realizability (CG1), geometric thickness of multigraphs (CG56), segment intersection
     graph (CG25).
(CG11) Arrangement Graph
Given: A graph G.
Question: Is G an arrangement graph? The vertices of an arrangement graph are intersection points of an
    arrangement L of lines in the plane, and two vertices are adjacent if and only if they lie on the same
    line of L and the line segment between them does not intersect any of the lines in L.

16.3     Covering and Packing
(CG16) Art Gallery Problem
Given: A simple polygon P with corners in Q2 and a number k ∈ N.
Question: Does there exist a set G ⊂ P of k guards such that every point inside the polygon is visible
     from G? Two points a, b are said to be visible to each other in case that the line segment ab is
     completely contained in the polygon P . The polygon is considered to be closed.
Complexity: ∃R-complete, by Abrahamsen, Adamaszek, Miltzow [AAM18, AAM22], and Stade [Sta23]
Comments: Also known as the minimum star cover problem [O’R87]. The original ∃R-completeness proof
     in [AAM22] is fairly involved, but Stade found a shorter proof in 2022 [Sch23a]. It is known that
     irrational coordinates can already be necessary for two and three guardable galleries [AAM17, MM22].
     There is a series of papers that try to find practical algorithms for the art gallery problem. Interestingly
     some of them come with provable performance guarantees under some mild assumptions [HM21].
Universality: The art gallery problem admits topological universality [BEMM+ 22, BEMM+ 23, ST22].
Open Questions: Does the problem lie in ∃R for semialgebraic art galleries, even in R2 ?
Also see: Polygon convex cover (CG19), star-shapedness of semialgebraic set (A-Open4).

(CG17) Boundary-Guarding
Given: A simple polygon P with corners in Q2 and a number k ∈ N.
Question: Does there exist a set G ⊂ ∂P of k guards such that every point inside the polygon is visible by
     at least one guard in G?
Complexity: ∃R-complete, by Stade [Sta23] via a reduction from RANGE-ETR-INV (L7).
Comments: The boundary guarding problems differs from the art gallery problem (CG16) in that the
     guards must be on the boundary.
Open Questions: It is open if boundary-boundary guarding is ∃R-complete; in the boundary-boundary
     variant, all guards must be placed on the boundary, and only the boundary has to be guarded [Sta23].
     This is similar to the terrain guarding problem, which turns out to be NP-complete [KK11, FHKS16].
Also see: Art gallery problem (CG16), ETR-INV (L5).

(CG18) Geometric Packing
Given: A simple polygon C, the container, and polygonal pieces p1 , . . . , pm , all polygons have corners in
    Q2 .
Question: Is it possible to move (translate and rotate) all the pieces so they lie in the container without
    overlapping?
Complexity: This problem is ∃R-complete, by Abrahamsen, Miltzow, and Seiferth [AMS20], even if the
    container is a square and all pieces are convex. The reduction is from ETR-INV (L5).
Comments: The problem is in NP in case that only translations are allowed. The proof from [AMS20]
    required that either the pieces or the container had a partially curved boundary. This condition was
    removed in a paper by Miltzow and Schmiermann [MS24] about continuous constraint satisfaction
    problems (L8), which implies that geometric packing remains ∃R-complete even if all the pieces are
    convex and polygonal, a simplified proof of that result can also be found in [AMS24].
Open Questions: Does the problem remain ∃R-hard if the pieces are restricted to a fixed number of shapes
    (one, for example) [Sch21b]? ▼ Is the problem fixed-parameter tractable in the number m of pieces?
    ▼ How hard is the packing problem if the pieces to be packed are unit disks? Hardness may be easier
    to show for polygons with holes [Abr24].

Question: Can the polygon be written as the union of at most k convex polygons?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Abrahamsen [Abr22] via a reduction from RANGE-ETR-INV (L7). The
    problem remains ∃R-complete even if all the convex polygons have to be triangles.

(CG32) Nerves of Convex Set
Given: A simplicial complex S of dimension k.
Question: Is S the k-skeleton of the nerve of c-dimensional convex sets in Rd ?
Complexity: ∃R-complete for many parameter combinations with k ≥ 2, in particular k ≥ d and c = d − 1
    or c = d, by Schnider and Weber [SW23].
Comments: This defines a family of problems. This family is parameterized by the dimension of the convex
    sets c, the ambient dimension d containing the convex sets and the dimension k of the dimension of
    the input simplicial complex. Note that for k = 1, this is a question about graphs. For example,
    (k, c, d) = (1, 1, 1) asks if the underlying graph is an interval graph, which is known to be polynomial
    time solvable [BL76]. Another illustrative example is (k, c, d) = (1, 1, 2). Here, we ask if the underlying
    graph is the intersection graph of segments, which is known to be ∃R-complete [KM94]. The hardness
    results stem from the hardness results of graphs combined with a lifting lemma due to Tancer [Tan10].
    Some other parameter combinations are always possible to realize (specifically d, c ≥ 2k + 1 [Weg67])
    and thus the computational problem becomes trivial.
     Given a family A of sets, we say the nerve of A is a simplicial complex that has one vertex for each
     member of A, and any subset B ⊆ A forms a simplex if their intersection is non-empty.
Open Questions: All remaining parameter combinations are still open.

16.5      Graph Drawing
       Graphs in this section are simple (no multiple edges, no loops) and undirected, unless we say
       otherwise. A (topological) drawing of a graph assigns a different location to each vertex of the
       graph, typically in R2 , and connects the endpoints of each edge by a (Jordan) curve. We assume
       that there are no vertices in the interior of edges, edges intersect finitely often, and no more than
       two edges cross in a point. In a geometric/straight-line drawing, all edges are represented by
       straight-line segments. We refer to crossing-free drawings as embeddings or planar.
       A rotation at a vertex is a cyclic permutation of the edges incident on the vertex (meant to
       represent the order in which the edges leave the vertex in a drawing or embedding). A rotation
       system assigns a rotation to each vertex of a graph.

16.6      Polytopes and Simplicial Complexes
       A polytope is the convex hull of a finite point set in Rd . The face lattice of a polytope is the lattice
       of its faces: the join of two faces is the smallest face containing both faces, and the meet is the
       intersection of the faces. Given a lattice, that is, a partial order with join and meet operations,
       one can ask whether it is polytopal, namely whether it is the face lattice of a polytope. We refer to
       the face lattice of P as its combinatorial type, and to P itself as a realization of this combinatorial
       type. The realizability question is known as the algorithmic Steinitz problem, due to a famous
       theorem of Steinitz. Let the graph of a polytope be the graph formed by the vertices and edges
       of the polytope. The graph is also referred to as the 1-skeleton, and the k-skeleton for k ≥ 1 is
       the complex of all faces of dimension up to k. Steinitz theorem characterizes the graphs of 3-
       dimensional polytopes: they are precisely the simple, planar, 3-connected graphs [Zie95, Section
       4], hence easy to recognize. For 3-polytopes the facial lattice is determined by the graph of the
       polytope, so the algorithmic Steinitz problem for 3-polytopes is tractable.
       Note that the complete combinatorial type of a polytope can be deduced from its set of (n − 1)-
       dimensional faces, or facets: the lower-dimensional faces are simply obtained by intersecting
       subsets of facets. The input to the problems can therefore be restricted to be a list of facets.



                                                          68
Schaefer, Cardinal, Miltzow                                                                   ∃R Compendium


     We obtain an interesting variant if we restrict the problem to simple polytopes, the skeletons of
     which are regular graphs. In that case the facial lattice is determined by the graph of the polytope
     (Blind and Mani with an easy proof by Kalai, see [Zie95, Section 3.4] and [KP03, Problem 15]).
     A polytope is said to be simplicial if all its facets are simplices.
     Subdivisions are closely related to polytopes. Given a set of points, a subdivision is a covering
     of their convex hull by polytopes, or cells, the vertices of which are points of the set, such that
     any two intersect in a common face. If all cells are simplices, then the subdivision is called a
     triangulation. A Delaunay subdivision is such that the cells are defined by an empty sphere
     condition: A cell C is part of the Delaunay subdivision of a set of points in Rd if and only if there
     exists a (d − 1)-sphere passing through the vertices of C but containing no other point of the set
     in its interior. For generic point sets, such cells are always simplices, and we talk of Delaunay
     triangulations.
     An abstract simplicial k-complex is a collection of sets of size at most k that is closed under
     taking subsets. More generally, an (abstract) polyhedral complex is a collection of (combinatorial
     types of) polytopes, such that every face of every polytope is also part of the collection, and any
     two polytopes in the collection intersect in a common face.

17.1      Games in Strategic Form
       We briefly recall the definitions related to games given in strategic form. An r-player game Γ in
       strategic form is a pair Γ = (Σi , Ui ), for i ∈ 1, 2, . . . , r, where Σi is the set of strategies available
       to the ith player, and Ui is the payoff function of player i, of the form Ui ∶ Σ1 × Σ2 × . . . × Σr → R.
       A mixed strategy for the ith player, as opposed to a pure strategy s ∈ Σi , is a probability distri-
       bution σi on the pure strategies in Σi . Let σ = (σi )i=1,2,...,r be a collection of mixed strategies for
       each of the r players. The expected payoff of the ith player under these probability distributions
       is:

       A Nash equilibrium is a collection of mixed strategies such that no player can improve her
       expected payoff by deviating from her current mixed strategy. Hence it consists of a collection of
       mixed strategies σ such that for every i ∈ {1, 2, . . . , r} and every σ ′ obtained by replacing σi by
       another mixed strategy σi′ , we have Ui (σ) ≥ Ui (σ ′ ). The classical result of Nash is that such an
       equilibrium exists for any game. A Nash equilibrium is said to be pure if it consists only of pure
       strategies.

(GT8) Trembling Hand Perfect Equilibrium
Given: A 3-player game Γ in strategic form, and a pure Nash equilibrium σ of Γ.

Given: A 3-player game Γ in strategic form, and a pure Nash equilibrium σ of Γ.

    given two pure strategies k and ℓ of the same player, if k is a worse reply against σ than ℓ, then σ must

17.2     Games in Extensive Form
       Games in extensive form are defined by a rooted tree with utility vectors at the leaves. Nodes of
       the tree are controlled either by one of the player, or by a so-called chance player, in which case
       we associate a probability distribution to the outgoing edges. In games in extensive form with
       imperfect information, strategies can only be based on partial information, or signals regarding
       the moves of the opponent. A behavioral strategy is a mixed strategy based only on the received
       signals. In games with imperfect recall, not only strategies can only be based on partial infor-
       mation, but players can forget about the sequence of signals or actions. The definitions extend
       to games that are defined on directed acyclic graphs. We refer to Hansen [Han19] and Gimbert,
       Paul, Srivathsan [GPS20] for detailed definitions.

(GT15) Trembling Hand Perfect Equilibrium for Games in Extensive Form

Question: Is σ a trembling hand perfect equilibrium?
Complexity: ∃R-complete by Hansen [Han19] via a reduction from Minmax value (GT7).
Comments: We refer [Sel75, vD84] for the definition of trembling hand perfect equilibria for games in
     extensive form. Hansen [Han19] also gives ∃R-completeness results for other properties of pure Nash
     equilibria of games in extensive form, in particular that of belonging to a sequential equilibrium [KW82]
     and being a quasi-perfect equilibrium [vD84].
Also see: Trembling Hand Perfect Equilibrium (GT8).

18      Machine Learning and Probabilistic Reasoning
       Artificial neural networks come in many variants. For the purpose of this section, we only define
       fully-connected, feed-forward, ReLU networks. Such a network realizes a parameterized function
       Np ∶ Rn → Rm which maps an input x ∈ Rn to some output Np (x) ∈ Rm given some parameters
       p (weights and biases). Given a set of data points (x, y), the goal is to find the right p such
       that Np predicts the y-values of the data points to within a given threshold. The function Np
       is the composition of two types of functions. The first type is a simple affine transformation
       x ↦ Ax + b. The second type is an activation function; examples include the identity function
       and the rectified linear unit activation function ReLU. (The name is more complicated than
       the function itself.) ReLU maps x ∈ Rn to y ∈ Rn , where yi = max(xi , 0). An artificial neural
       network can be described as a repeated composition of affine functions and ReLU’s. We refer
       the interested reader to the comprehensive book by Goodfellow, Bengio and Aaron on Deep
       learning [GBC16], for an in-depth introduction of the great variety neural network architectures
       and training methods.

       When we want to reason about probabilities in a formal sense, we can define formal languages
       L which can express probabilities of events, where events can again be combined using elemen-
       tary variables, conditional probabilities and conjunction of events, comparison of probabilities,
       independence statements, confirmation statements and potentially many more. There is an illus-
       trative example that shows us that irrational numbers might be needed to find a solution. We
       try to find probabilities
                             √ such that Pr(A ∩ B) = 1 − Pr(A ∩ B) and Pr(A ∩ B) = Pr(B) ⋅ Pr(B)
       implies that Pr(B) = 1/2.

(CG-Open17) Graph Flattenability
Given: A graph G, integer d ≥ 0.
Question: For every straight-line embedding of G in Rd , with arbitrary d′ ≥ d, is there a straight-line
                                                           ′


     embedding in Rd with the same distances between all pairs of vertices?
Complexity: The problem lies in ∀∃R [BC07] (the authors observe that it is equivalent to testing the
     equality of two semialgebraic sets). For fixed d, graph flattenability is minor-closed and can therefore
     be solved in polynomial time; for hardness results it will therefore be essential that d is part of the
     input. Lists of excluded minors are known for d ≤ 3 [BC07].

(CG-Open18) Faithful Drawability of Edge-Colored Graph
Given: A graph G and a proper edge-coloring of G, that is, any two adjacent edges differ in color.
Question: Is there a faithful drawing of G, that is, a drawing of G in which all edges of the same color lie
     on concurrent lines, and no two edges lie on the same line?
Complexity: In ∃R, but otherwise open even for 4-regular graphs.
Comments: Richter shows that faithful drawability can be recognized in polynomial time for cubic graphs
     and conjectures that the problem is ∃R-complete for 4=regular graphs [Ric11, Conjecture 9]. By moving
     the common points of the bundles of concurrent lines to infinity, we obtain a drawing in which all edges
     of the same color are parallel; this seems to suggest a connection to the planar slope number (CG40).
Also see: Planar slope number (CG40).

(CG-Open19) Kissing Number
Given: A compact semialgebraic set S ⊆ Rn , an integer k ≥ 0..
Question: Are there k non-overlapping congruent copies of S each touching S? The largest such k is the
     kissing number of S.
Complexity: Open.
Comments: For many natural geometric sets, such as polygons or spheres, there are known upper bounds
     on the kissing number, which places the problem in ∃R, so solvers can, in principle, be used to find
     the kissing number in those instances. A similar problem, the largest number of pairwise touching
     non-overlapping congruent copies of cylinders, was tackled using a similar, but more sophisticated
     approach, see [BLR15].
Also see: Unit disk contact graph (CG-Open3).

(CG-Open20) Euclidean Minimum Spanning Tree
Given: A tree T .
Question: Is T the Euclidean minimum spanning tree of a set of points in the plane? In the Euclidean

Complexity: In ∃R and known to be NP-hard by Eades and Whitesides [EW96a].
Comments: The maximum degree of T has to be 6, since every tree of maximum degree 5 is a Euclidean
    Minimum Spanning Tree; the construction showing this requires a double-exponential grid; as far as

(CG-Open21) Nearest Neighbor Graph
Given: A graph G.
Question: Is G the nearest neighbor graph of a set of points in the plane? The nearest-neighbor graph of
     a point set has a vertex for each point, and there is an edge between two vertices if they are nearest
     neighbors to each other. Here p is a nearest neighbor of q if there is no point closer to p than q.
Complexity: In ∃R and known to be NP-hard by Eades and Whitesides [EW96b].
Comments: There are several variants of this problem, the variant we presented here is called the mutual
     nearest neighbor graph in [EW96b].
Also see: Euclidean minimum spanning tree (CG-Open20), Gabriel graph (CG-Open22).

(CG-Open22) Gabriel Graph
Given: A graph G.
Question: Is G a Gabriel graph in the plane? The Gabriel graph of a point set has a vertex for each point,
     and there is an edge between two vertices pq if the disk with diameter pq contains no other vertices of
     the graph.
Complexity: In ∃R and known to be NP-hard by Eades and Whitesides [EW96b].
Comments: The realization of a Gabriel graph contains the Euclidean minimum spanning tree (CG-
     Open20) and the nearest neighborhood graph (CG-Open21) of the point set, and is itself a subset
     of the Delaunay triangulation (CG72).
Also see: Euclidean minimum spanning tree (CG-Open20), nearest neighbor graph (CG-Open21), Delaunay
     triangulation (CG72).

(CG-Open23) Hidden Set in Polygon
Given: A simple polygon P , natural number k ≥ 0.
Question: Are there k points inside the region enclosed by P which cannot pairwise see each other?
Complexity: Known to be NP-hard by Eidenbenz [Eid02] and to lie in ∃R [Fan20].
Comments: As with visibility graphs one can consider variants in which the hidden points must lie on the
     boundary or the polygon has holes. There are also variants based on terrains rather than polygons.
     (This problem is also sometimes called the bird nesting box problem. The idea is that you want to place
     as many bird nesting boxes as possible. However, if two bird nesting boxes see each other they may be
     avoided by birds as many bird species avoid other birds.)
Also see: Visibility graphs (CG35).

(CG-Open24) Watchman Route Problem
Given: A polygon with holes, an integer k ≥ 0.
Question: Is there a polygonal curve of length at most k such that every point of the polygon can be seen
     from some point on the polygonal curve?
Complexity: In ∃R, as shown by Volk [Vol23]. NP-hardness is shown by Dumitrescu and Tóth [DT12], who
     explain why the earlier NP-hardness proof by Chin and Ntafos [CN88], in the paper that introduced
     the problem, does not work. The problem is polynomial-time solvable for simple polygons, see [DT12]
     for more background.
Comments: The definition of the problem only gives ∃∀R-membership, showing the problem lies in ∃R
     requires additional analysis. Volk [Vol23] also considers the variant in which the polygonal curve has
     at most k bends.
Open Questions: What is the complexity of the problem in unbounded dimension? In that case, ∃∀R is
     the best upper bound.
Also see: Lawn moving problem (CG-Open25) art gallery problem (CG16), visibility graph of polygon with
     holes (CG36).

(CG-Open26) Sweeping Points
Given: Finite set P ⊆ Q2 , ℓ ∈ Q≥0 .
Question: Can all the points be swept to the origin using sweeps of total length at most ℓ? In a single
    sweep, an infinite line is moved in parallel from one location to another location (the distance swept
    is the contribution of that sweep to the total length). Points encountered along the sweep get moved
    with the line.
Comments: Dumitrescu and Jiang [DJ11] attribute this problem to Paweł Żyliński; they study approxi-
    mation algorithms, and ask whether it can be solved in polynomial time.
Open Questions: Can the shortest length solution always be achieved in a polynomial number of sweeps [DJ11]?

(CG-Open27) Hypercube
Given: Finite set of points P ⊆ [0, 1]d , a natural number k ∈ N.
Question: Is there a pointset Q ⊆ [0, 1]d of size k such that P ⊂ conv(Q), where conv(Q) is the convex hull
     of Q?
Complexity: The hypercube problem is NP-hard via a reduction from 3SAT, and lies in ∃R as shown by
     Kiefer and Wacther [KW14]. Kiefer and Wachter also observe that for fixed d, the problem lies in P.
Comments: The problem remains NP-hard if P is required to contain the origin, the restricted hypercube
     problem. Kiefer and Wachter introduced this problem to isolate the geometric difficulty at the root of
     the probabilitic automaton minimisation problem (ML-Open1). The hypercube problem is reminiscent
     of the nested polytope problem (CG71) as defined by [DHM19].
Open Questions: Kiefer and Wachter [KW14] observe that for d = 2 the set Q can always be assumed to
     be rational, and ask whether this remains true for higher dimensions.
Also see: Probabilitic automaton minimisation (ML-Open1), nested polytope problem (CG71).

(CG-Open28) k-Median of Polygonal Curves
Given: A family of polygonal curves P1 , . . . , Pn in Rd , all of the same length, c ∈ Q.
Question: Is there a polygonal curve P of length k such that ∑i∈[n] dF (P, Pi ) ≤ c? Here, dF denotes the
     Fréchet distance, see references for a definition.
Complexity: In ∃R, as shown by Rohde [Roh22], and NP-hard by Buchin, Driemel, and Struijs [BDS20].
Comments: The Fréchet distance between two polygonal curves can be computed efficiently [AG92].

(CG-Open29) Fréchet Distance of Surfaces
Given: Two homeomorphic surfaces R and S together with immersions φR ∶ R → R3 , and φS ∶ S ⇒ R3 ,
    δ ∈ Q≥0 .
Question: Is the Fréchet distance δF (R, S) ≤ δ? Here δF (R, S) is the infimum over all homeomorphisms
    f ∶ R → S of supx∈R ∥φR (x) − φS (f (x))∥2 .
Complexity: One has to assume that R, S, φR and φS have reasonable effective representations for this
    problem to fall into the domain of ∃R. There are various relevant results, e.g. Godau’s proof that the
    problem is NP-hard [God99], and Nayyeri and Xu’s result that the problem lies in ∃R if one of the
    surfaces is a triangle [NX18].

(CG-Open30) Compatible Triangulations of Polygons with Holes
Given: Two vertex-labeled polygons P and Q with holes, an integer k ≥ 0.
Question: Can P and Q be extended to vertex-labeled triangulations which are compatible by adding at
    most k points? Here two triangulations are compatible if they have the same rotation system, that is,
    the cyclic permutations of neighbors at each vertex is the same for both triangulations.
Complexity: In ∃R and NP-hard, as shown by Lubiw and Mondal [LM20], who also ask whether the
    problem is ∃R-hard.
Comments: The additional points are known as Steiner points; the given polygons have to be compatible
    to start with for the problem to be solvable.

    gons (no holes).

Given: A family of point sets in Q2 .
Question: Can the point sets be translated so that the resulting points are in convex position, that is, lie

(CG-Open35) Obstacle Number
Given: A graph G, an integer k ≥ 0.

     does not intersect any obstacles.

Given: A graph G, an integer k ≥ 0.
Question: Is there a k-treetope polytope P with 1-skeleton G? A k-treetope is a k-dimensional polytope

22.5    Machine Learning and Probabilistic Reasoning
(ML-Open1) Probabilistic Automaton Minimisation
Given: A probabilistic automaton A, a natural number n ∈ N.
Question: Does there exists a probabilistic automaton A′ of size n so that A and A′ are equivalent?
Complexity: The problem was shown to be NP-hard by Kiefer and Wachter [KW14] via a reduction from
     the restricted hypercube problem (CG-Open27), which is known to be NP-hard [KW14]. The problem
     is known to be contained in ∃R [KW14].

     lem (CG71), so there is hope to strengthen the result to ∃R-completeness.

22.6    Markov Chains and Decision Processes
(MDP-Open1) Universal Safety for Probabilistic Finite State Automata
Given: A probabilistic finite state automata A [AGV18] and a safety polytope H given by its vertex
    representation.
Question: Is it true that for every starting distribution there exists a strategy such that A stays in the
    safety polytope H?
Complexity: Akshay, Genest, and Vyas show that the problem lies in ∃R [AGV18].
Comments: The problem has many variants. One can ask for existential safety instead of universal safety,
